answer:
English is almost impossible to avoid in everyday life today. We hear it on television and in song lyrics, study it at school, and, for many of us, use it at work. This constant exposure gives us a fairly good sense of how the language works. I think most people can understand at least some English, and quite a few probably have an excellent command of it. However, when I consider my own abilities, some areas are clearly more challenging than others. I feel more confident in the receptive skills of reading and listening, while writing and speaking are more difficult for me.

Throughout my years of studying English, first in primary school and then in secondary school, my teachers consistently emphasised writing. In secondary school in particular, we wrote many essays and various kinds of reviews. Yet despite having had considerable practice in writing English, I still encounter difficulties. Spelling can sometimes be challenging, but grammatical errors are a greater concern for me. In my experience, grammatical problems are often complicated and harder to resolve than spelling difficulties, which can usually be settled by looking up a word in a dictionary.

We did not get much reading practice at school. Of course, we had textbooks, but the articles were often very short and covered unrelated topics, making them feel disconnected and lacking in context. In other words, the textbooks were boring. Apart from these texts, we also read several works of literature and wrote reviews of them. I think reading literature is a tremendously rewarding way to develop fluency in a language. This experience also proved valuable when I studied religious studies, as much of the required reading was in English.

My greatest difficulty when reading English arises when a text contains specialised terminology. Reading an English text that would probably be challenging even in Swedish is both demanding and time-consuming. This brings me to another problem: my patience, or rather my lack of it. Naturally, reading in English takes longer than reading in Swedish, at least initially, but for some reason I find that difficult to accept.

Speaking and listening are obviously closely related. Nevertheless, I find listening the easiest of the four language skills and speaking the most difficult. This is undoubtedly because I get far more practice in listening, particularly through television and music, than in speaking. Although I do not understand every word, I can usually follow what is being said. Specialised language, however, presents difficulties in listening as well as in reading.

As I mentioned earlier, speaking is my greatest challenge in English. I have had little practical experience because I have never spent an extended period abroad. Since English teaching at school focused primarily, or even exclusively, on theory, I had little opportunity to practise speaking there either. If anything, school can make students even more reluctant to speak: we become so preoccupied with grammatical accuracy that we are afraid to open our mouths for fear of being laughed at. I know this sounds rather bleak, and it probably does not reflect everyone’s experience. Nevertheless, I believe these fears would soon fade with regular speaking practice.

Having completed this assignment, I realise how difficult it is to assess my own abilities in the four language skills. I have never struggled to achieve good grades in English, but I firmly believe that grades rarely reveal much about a person’s actual knowledge. What I do know is that learning a language involves many different skills, and I would like to improve in all of them.
